Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions

passages.text: Probiotics are colonies of live microorganisms that offer quantifiable health benefits. By regulating the gut microbiota, they could maintain intestinal barrier function, regulate immune function, and stimulate the generation of circulating metabolites that exert systemic effects. Bifidobacterium constitutes one of the most significant bacterial taxa in the human intestine, with its characteristics and mechanisms of action having been extensively documented since 1950. Over the past two decades, multiple probiotic candidates from the Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus genera have been shown in experimental and clinical studies to reduce manifestations associated with intestinal injury. A recent study found that male mice with Bifidobacterium supplementation showed a reduction in the damage to the high-fat diet-driven impairment of the gut barrier. A random trial involving 100 students with diarrhea showed that taking Bifidobacterium could effectively alleviate diarrhea symptoms and restore the disrupted intestinal flora caused by diarrhea. Furthermore, our group's previous research demonstrated that Lactobacillus johnsonii BS15 could restore ileal microbial dysbiosis, heightened intestinal permeability, and aberrant inflammatory responses resulting from fluoride exposure in drinking water, concurrently ameliorating hippocampal injury in mice. This suggests that probiotic intervention in the ileum could offer a means of preventing and treating intestinal and extraintestinal diseases induced by fluoride. However, even when classified within a single species, distinct probiotic strains could display markedly divergent characteristics and may yield substantially different clinical outcomes. Consequently, further investigation is required to establish the effectiveness of a beneficial probiotic strain. Discovering and studying the probiotic properties of more bacterial strains in specific application scenarios not only provides more bacterial strain resources, but also offers more possibilities for future disease prevention and treatment.

The potential beneficial impacts of B. animalis subsp. animalis GY007 on ileal dysfunction and ecological imbalance caused by fluoride were assessed in this study. Our research may offer a conceptual framework to support the use of probiotic interventions for managing the intestinal injury associated with excessive fluoride exposure.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Bacterial Strain and Culture

The strain GY007 was stored in the China center for type culture collection with preservation number CCTCC AB 2025172. GY007 was purified and inoculated into the prepared culture medium broth at 37  C for 24 h and subcultured for three generations, to ensure activity. The third-generation bacterial suspension was centrifuged at 4000 g for 15 min and resuspended in normal saline, which was repeated three times for washing. The concentration of GY007 was adjusted to 1 x 109 CFU mL-1 using the colony counting method for in vivo experiments.
2.2. Animal and Experiment Design

As shown in Figure 1A, the C57BL/6J mice (male, 3 weeks old) were procured from Si Pei Fu and maintained under standard caging conditions. Throughout the experiment, animals were housed under standardized housing parameters (20-22  C) with a 12:12 h light-dark cycle, and six mice were accommodated in each cage. Mice were maintained with free access to standard chow and water (i.e., food and water were continuously available and not restricted) and monitored daily for health. Following a 7-day acclimation period, the animals were randomly allocated to three groups (n = 12 per group): a control group (Ctrl), a fluoride-exposed group (F), and a fluoride-exposed group supplemented with GY007 (F+Bi). All treatments were administered once daily via oral gavage, with the following treatment. The F+Bi group received sequential gavage of two 0.2 mL preparations: a fluoride solution (24 mg/kg, dissolved in normal saline) and a GY007 bacterial suspension (1 x 109 CFU/mL, prepared in normal saline). The F group was gavaged with an identical volume of the fluoride solution (0.2 mL), followed by 0.2 mL of normal saline. The Ctrl group was administered an equivalent total volume of normal saline alone. All the experimental procedures lasted for eight weeks. The doses of fluoride solution and duration of the experiment were as given in previous studies.

On the final day of the 8-week experimental period, blood was collected by retro-orbital sampling from mice. The blood samples were centrifuged to isolate the serum, which was then stored at -80  C for testing. All mice were culled by cervical dislocation and sampling was conducted immediately. The ileum was excised and opened; luminal contents were gently scraped into sterile tubes. Ileal contents were promptly frozen at -80  C for subsequent 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing and non-targeted metabolomics. The collected ileal tissue was flushed with ice-cold saline, cut into small pieces and immediately stored at -80  C for testing. All procedures were performed on ice. The partial ileal tissue without intraluminal material was in 4% paraformaldehyde solution and partial ileal tissues containing luminal content were in methanol-carnoy for at least 24 h for fixation.
2.3. Metabolite Detection and Bioinformatics Analysis

A total of 24 ileal contents samples were performed to untargeted metabolite profiling, with 8 samples per group. Metabolite profiling and the associated bioinformatics workflows were carried out in accordance with procedures reported previously.
2.4. 16S rRNA Sequencing and Analysis

A total of 24 ileal contents samples were performed to 16S rRNA sequencing, with 8 samples per group, corresponding to the metabolite detection samples. Briefly, ileal content DNA was extracted using the E.Z.N.A. Stool DNA Kit. The V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified with barcoded primers 338F/806R, and amplicons were purified, quantified, pooled in equimolar amounts, and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform (2 x 250 bp, paired-end). Reads were processed in QIIME2 2024.5 for demultiplexing, primer trimming, quality control, and denoising/merging/chimera removal with DADA2; ASVs were aligned with MAFFT and a phylogeny was built with FastTree2. Taxonomy was assigned using a Naive Bayes classifier against Greengenes2 2022.10. Alpha diversity (Shannon, Simpson), beta diversity (Bray-Curtis; PCoA), and PERMANOVA were performed in QIIME2 and R V4.3.3. Random forest was used to discriminate groups, and Mantel and Spearman correlation analyses were applied to assess microbiota-metabolome and phenotype associations. Detailed information is provided in the Supplementary File S1.
2.5. Real-Time Quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) of mRNA Expression Levels

Five specimens from each experimental group were randomly chosen (15 in total) for RNA isolation in this part. Total RNA from ileal tissue was extracted using procedures that have been reported previously. Primer information is provided in Supplementary Table S1.
2.6. Histology

The subsequent steps were the same as described in the previous research. The anti-MUC2 (1:500), anti-4-HNE (1:100), anti-ZO-1 (1:100), anti-Claudin-1 (1:50), anti-Occludin (1:500), anti-IRF7 (1:1000), anti-TLR9 (1:100), anti-NF-kappab (1:1000), anti-IRAK4 (1:1000), and anti-Myd88 (1:200) were used to assess the condition of the ileal tissue.
2.7. Biochemical Analysis

The serum samples and the ileal tissue were estimated. The blood samples were centrifuged at 3000x g for 15 min at 4  C. Subsequently, serum diamine oxidase (DAO) and D-lactate were measured using mouse-specific ELISA kits (Jiangsu Enzyme Technology, Yancheng, Jiangsu, China). Antioxidant indices in the ileal tissue were measured using commercial kits (Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, Jiangsu, China), including total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC; A015-3-1), catalase (CAT; A007-1-1), reduced glutathione (GSH; A006-2-1), malondialdehyde (MDA; A003-1-2), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2; A064-1-1), and superoxide dismutase (SOD; A001-3-2).
2.8. Statistical Analysis

Normal distributions were assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk normality test. If the data were not normally distributed, normality tests were repeated after log-transformation. Normally distributed data with homogeneity of variance were analyzed using t-tests (two independent samples) or one-way ANOVA with LSD post hoc multiple analysis (comparisons among multiple groups). Normally distributed data with heterogeneity of variance among multiple groups were analyzed using one-way ANOVA with Dunnett's T3 post hoc analysis. Data that did not reach a normal distribution were tested using the Kruskal-Wallis test at p < 0.05, followed by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Data are presented as the mean +- standard deviation and were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 27. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, and *** p < 0.001 were considered significant. The mapping software used was GraphPad Software 8.0.
3. Results
3.1. GY007 Could Alleviate Intestinal Barrier Damage Induced by Fluoride

Consistent with the animal handling protocol outlined above, serum samples were obtained from the mice (Figure 1A). As illustrated in Figure 1B,C, the F group exhibited markedly (p < 0.001) higher levels of D-lactate and DAO than control mice. Mice receiving GY007 (F+Bi) displayed reduced circulating D-lactate and DAO concentrations, relative to the F group (p < 0.05). For both parameters, the Ctrl and F+Bi groups did not differ significantly (p > 0.05). Tight junction proteins were assessed in the ileal tissue of the mice. In the F group, both mRNA expression and protein levels of Claudin-1 (Figure 2A,B), Occludin (Figure 2D,E) and ZO-1 (Figure 2G,H) were markedly decreased in comparison to the remaining groups (p < 0.05). Treatment of GY007 significantly restored these markers (p < 0.05), with no significant difference observed between the Ctrl and F+Bi (p > 0.05). To evaluate the in situ expression patterns of these proteins, immunofluorescence staining was carried out thereafter. As depicted in Figure 2C,F,I, a significant decrease in these proteins was detected in the F group versus Ctrl, while GY007 administration restored their expression to levels comparable with those observed in controls. Overall, the results indicated that fluoride would cause enhanced intestinal permeability of the ileum and decreased expression of tight junction proteins, while GY007 could inhibit this negative impact.
3.2. GY007 Could Repair the Ileal Oxidative Damage Induced by Fluoride

Analyses were conducted to further evaluate the oxidative stress profile in the mouse ileum. Significant variations (p < 0.05) of SOD (Figure 3B) and CAT (Figure 3D) activities together with MDA (Figure 3A), T-AOC (Figure 3C), and H2O2 (Figure 3E) contents were observed in the F group. Administration of GY007 significantly modulated MDA, SOD, T-AOC, and CAT measurements (p < 0.01), restoring these indices to values that were not statistically different from those in the Ctrl group with no significant difference observed between the Ctrl and F+Bi (p > 0.05). Although GY007 treatment was able to significantly reverse (p < 0.05) the trend of fluoride-induced accumulation of H2O2 in the ileum, H2O2 levels remained substantially higher than the Ctrl group (p < 0.05). Meanwhile, across the groups, no statistically meaningful differences were observed, regardless of whether fluoride exposure or GY007 dosing was applied (p > 0.05, Figure 3F). Then, the mRNA expressions of Duox2 and Duoxa2 were detected. As presented in Figure 3G,H, fluoride exposure led to significantly upregulated (p < 0.05) ileal Duox2 and Duoxa2 mRNA levels relative to the Ctrl group, while GY007 could significantly reverse (p < 0.01) this trend. Further immunofluorescence results confirmed that the lipid peroxidation reaction in the F group was enhanced. The use of GY007 could reduce the lipid peroxidation reaction in the ileum of mice (Figure 3I). In aggregate, these data implied that fluoride causes oxidative stress damage to the ileum of mice, while the use of GY007 could partially alleviate these adverse effects.
3.3. The Influences of Fluoride Exposure and Probiotic GY007 on Function and Mucus Layer of the Ileum

Reg3a, b, g, MUC2 and Ramp1 are important indicators for characterizing intestinal homeostasis and function. Therefore, the mRNA expression levels of them were further examined. After fluoride treatment, ileal mRNA levels of Reg3a, b, g and MUC2 were reduced, consistent with a loss of intestinal homeostasis (p < 0.01, Figure 4A-D). The application of GY007 could significantly reverse the transcriptional levels of them (p < 0.05) to values comparable with the Ctrl group (except for Reg3a). Immunofluorescence analyses suggested that the staining intensity of MUC2 and Ramp1 were diminished in the ileum of mice exposed to fluoride, while the use of GY007 could enhance the expression (Figure 4E,F). MUC2 serves as a key scaffolding element within the external mucous barrier layer. More detailed examination of the defining features of mucus in the ileum was observed. Evaluating intestinal mucus characteristics in fixed tissue slices remains difficult, largely because mucus preservation in fixed specimens is inconsistent. Fixed sections from the Ctrl, F, and F+Bi groups were subjected to Alcian blue-periodic acid-Schiff (AB/PAS) staining and inspected to assess whether fluoride treatment and GY007 administration produced changes in the intestinal mucus (Figure 4G). In comparison with the Ctrl, the surface of the ileal villi and the mucus in the inter-villus spaces in the F group decreased, while the F+Bi group showed a trend toward restoration. Glycogen, neutral mucoprotein, and various glycoproteins appear purple-red, while acidic mucoprotein, proteoglycan and hyaluronic acid appear blue in the AB/PAS staining. The mucin components in the F group were particularly different, more resembling acidic mucopolysaccharides, while the F+Bi group and the Ctrl group were more similar to neutral mucopolysaccharides. These results suggeste that fluoride exposure compromises the intestinal homeostasis, function and mucus properties of the ileum, while GY007 could produce a positive effect.
3.4. Impacts of Fluoride Exposure and GY007 on Toll-like Receptor (TLR) Signaling Pathway and Downstream Inflammatory-Related Factors

TLR-mediated signaling has been widely investigated as a key mechanism through which probiotics influence host regulatory processes. The interaction between them could trigger local immune responses in the intestine, which may affect the homeostasis and communication within the body. This part focused on the levels of key components within the TLR signaling pathway of the ileum in mice (Figure S1). As shown in Figure 5A-F, GY007 significantly decreased the mRNA expression and protein content of TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IFN-alpha within the murine ileum (p < 0.01), restoring them to levels not significantly different from those of the control mice. We detected IL17, IL-10, and IFN-gamma, additionally (Figure 5G-I). Fluoride administration markedly elevated (p < 0.01) the level of mRNA expression of IL-17 in the ileum. GY007 had a reversing trend but no statistical significance (p = 0.062). Across the three groups, IL-10 and IFN-gamma levels did not differ significantly (p > 0.05). As shown in Figure 6, GY007 significantly attenuated the fluoride-induced upregulation of ileal IRAK4, IRF7, Myd88, NF-kappab, and TLR9 mRNA levels (p < 0.05). Immunofluorescence assay showed a trend consistent with the mRNA expression levels. Notably, the mRNA levels of TLR2, TLR3, TLR5, TLR7, and TLR8 did not differ significantly across the experimental groups (p > 0.05, Figure S2A-E). In the F group, TLR4 mRNA expression was markedly elevated (p < 0.05), while GY007 showed a tendency towards a decrease that did not achieve statistical significance (Figure 2F). These results suggest that GY007 may modulate the changes in TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IFN-alpha levels caused by fluoride exposure through TLR9, although a direct causal relationship has not been functionally validated.
3.5. GY007 Could Restore Microbial Structure in High Fluoride Exposure-Induced Ileal Injury

To explore the function of probiotics from a microbiological perspective, the 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing of the ileal content was conducted. Rarefaction analysis assessed the observed species across the collected samples. The findings indicated that, in each of the three cohorts, the accumulation of detected genes approached a plateau, suggesting that sequencing depth was sufficient to capture most of the measurable diversity (Figure S3A). As illustrated in Figure 7A, alpha diversity analysis showed that the F group had a significantly lower Simpson index than the Ctrl group (p < 0.05). In contrast, the Shannon diversity index exhibited a decreasing trend in the F group, although this change did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05). GY007 could significantly reverse the reduction in diversity caused by fluoride (p < 0.05). As shown in Figure 7B, the microbial communities among the three groups each exhibited unique patterns (p < 0.001, R2 = 0.46). The intestinal microbial distribution structure of F+Bi was more similar to that of the control. Analysis at the phylum-level profiling indicated that the ileal microbiome mainly comprised Firmicutes_D, Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Desulfobacterota_I, and Firmicutes_A (Figure 7C). It is worth noting that the abundances of Firmicutes_A and Actinobacteriota within the mouse ileum was significantly changed after fluoride exposure (p < 0.001), while GY007 could significantly reverse this trend (p < 0.05, Figure S3B). Genus-level composition in the top five genera predominantly comprised Lactobacillus, Limosilactobacillus, Dubosiella, Bifidobacterium, and Ligilactobacillus (Figure 7D). Both the LEfSe procedure and a random forest model from machine learning workflows provided additional evidence of pronounced differences in gut microbial composition across the three groups. Also, seven biomarkers were simultaneously identified by both methods (Figure 7E,F and Figure S3C). Within the set of marker genera identified, in comparison with the control mice, fluoride exposure significantly altered the abundance of the majority of these taxa (p < 0.01, Figure 7G). Although there was no statistical significance, the presence of GY007 tended to make the abundances of these markers closer to those of the Ctrl group, even in Dubosiella (Figure 7G). These observations indicated that fluoride exposure may disrupt the diversity and structure of the ileum microbiota, whereas GY007 could relieve this condition.
3.6. Effects of GY007 on Ileal Metabolic Profiles in Mice Subjected to Fluoride Exposure

To assess ileal metabolic alterations in fluoride-exposed mice following administration of GY007, the metabolomics analysis was conducted. In total, 2479 metabolites were detected, comprising 1224 acquired in positive ion (POS) and 1255 acquired in negative ion (NEG). Based on LC-MS-derived ileal profiles, the PCA score plots demonstrated distinct clustering of the Ctrl and F groups in both of the ion acquisition modes (Figure 8A,B). Following GY007 administration, samples from the F+Bi group generally shifted away from the F group in the multivariate space, although partial overlap persisted (Figure 8C,D). These findings suggested that GY007 administration partially mitigates fluoride-induced metabolic dysfunction and may confer a protective effect on the ileum. To identify metabolites exhibiting statistically significant differences across the three groups, variables meeting the thresholds of a VIP > 1 and a p < 0.05 were selected as differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs). A total of 295 DEMs were detected in the F versus F+Bi contrast; 346 DEMs were found when comparing Ctrl with F (Figure 8E, Tables S2 and S3). When evaluating the differences between the Ctrl and F groups, 169 were upregulated and 177 were downregulated in the F group (Figure 8E, Table S2). When evaluating differences between the F and F+Bi group, 175 were downregulated and 120 were upregulated in the F+Bi group (Figure 8F, Table S3). The Venn diagram in Figure 8G shows that the 111 common DEMs were detected in both comparisons (Figure 8E). The expression profiles of 27 upregulated and 21 downregulated metabolites in F were significantly restored in the F+Bi. We focused on the changes of nine specific DEMs. The accumulation of hippuric acid could lead to the excessive production of the total in vivo level of reactive oxygen species. Isocytosine is the positional isomer of cytosine and is involved in the metabolism of bacteria. MN6249 (hippuric acid, HIA) and MP3188 (isocytosine, ISO) were observed to increase in F and decrease in F+Bi (p < 0.01, Figure 8F,G). The concentration of bile acids in the mice exposed to the fluoride environment is worthy of attention. As shown in Figure 8H-K, four bile acids, alcohols and their derivatives, including MN18188 (TRI), MN18722 (OIC-7alpha), MP21633 (OIC-3), and MP22898 (OIC-3alpha), showed a significant reduction in the F group (p < 0.05). GY007 could reverse this trend (p < 0.05). 18-Glycyrrhetinic acid, Saikosaponin B2 and Sinapinic acid could have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant stress effects. GY007 could markedly reverse (p < 0.05) the decrease in the abundance of MN19753 (18-Glycyrrhetinic acid, GLA), MP26064 (Saikosaponin B2, SAB), and MP9998 (sinapinic acid, SIA) caused by fluoride (Figure 8L-N). Based on the 13 markers for inflammatory bowel disease identified by the cohorts, seven of them were annotated and evaluated in this study. Except for MN6908 (L-Carnitine) and MN7724 (L-Tryptophan), the remaining metabolites showed no significant differences among the three groups (Figure S4). Bubble plots were employed to depict the key metabolic pathways most strongly enriched by the identified biomarkers in the two comparisons (Figure 8O,P). The metabolites of Ctrl vs. F were mainly involved in bile secretion, ABC transporters, and histidine metabolism (Figure 8O). There were four pathways enriched in F vs. F+Bi, namely purine metabolism, histidine metabolism, longevity regulating pathway, and arachidonic acid metabolism (Figure 8P).
3.7. Relevance Analysis of the Microbiota and Metabolism with Ileal Function Variables

To clarify how ileal molecules may mediate the probiotic-driven restoration of fluoride-induced intestinal injury, we integrated the datasets generated above:namely, key genera identified by 16S rRNA sequencing and representative DEMs from the metabolomics screen:and subsequently performed Pearson correlation and Mantel test analyses. As shown in Figure 9A, the obtained results confirmed that there was an interesting correlation between the metabolite groups, the bacterial genus groups and the key indicators. Myd88 and TNF-alpha-mRNA are the most explanatory variables in the case of probiotics reversing fluoride-induced intestinal damage (for Myd88, the genus: Mantel's r = 0.63; the metabolites: Mantel's r = 0.59; for TNF-alpha-mRNA, the genus: Mantel's r = 0.60 and the metabolites: Mantel's r = 0.58; all p < 0.01), with MDA and Occludin protein levels being the next most significant (p < 0.01). There was an expected correlation among the indicators of intestinal function. Furthermore, we conducted Spearman analysis to evaluate the correlations between each key factor in the metabolites, the genus and the intestinal function indicators, separately. As shown in Figure 9B, among the 30 indicators related to the function of the ileum, seven key bacterial genera were correlated with at least sixteen of the indicators, while nine key metabolites were correlated with at least three of the indicators. The Bifidobacterium, MP3188 (ISO), MN18722 (OIC-7alpha), and MP9998 (SIA) showed a closer correlation with more of the aforementioned experimental indicators. It is worth noting that Mantel and Spearman analyses indicate co-variation, not directionality.
4. Discussion

High fluoride-associated disorders constitute some of the most prevalent and severe endemic conditions worldwide, with particularly pronounced impacts on the gastrointestinal tract. Consequently, strategies focused on mitigating fluoride-induced ileal injury have become a major area of research interest and significance. Probiotic-based interventions offer a promising approach to alleviating intestinal injury. The therapeutic effect of B. animalis subsp. animalis GY007 on high fluoride-induced intestinal damage in mice was evaluated. A review of the existing literature revealed the absence of a universally accepted standard for determining high fluoride exposure concentrations. The chosen dosage of 24 mg/kg body weight NaF and the duration were determined in accordance with our earlier investigations and other published research. According to the dose conversion formula of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the equivalent human dose is approximately 23.8 mg/L for an adult weighing 55 kg and with a daily water intake of 4.5 L. In contrast, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a guideline value for fluoride in drinking water of 1.5 mg/L, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) primary maximum contaminant level (MCL) is 4.0 mg/L. In practice, the primary strategy to mitigate fluoride-related health risks is to reduce fluoride intake. Where low fluoride water or foods are not readily achievable, our findings suggest that GY007 could be explored as an adjunct, diet-deliverable approach to support intestinal barrier function during high fluoride exposure, rather than as a substitute for source control. Bifidobacterium animalis strains have been used as probiotic ingredients in foods and dietary supplements under FDA "no questions" GRAS notices, and they have also been officially included in the "List of Microorganisms Approved for Use in Food," published by the National Health Commission (NHC), supporting their feasibility as a food ingredient. Future work should include dose optimization and human studies in fluoride-exposed populations, incorporating clinically relevant outcomes (e.g., gastrointestinal symptoms and stool microbiome profiles).

Increased intestinal epithelial permeability is a critical determinant in the pathogenesis of various gastrointestinal disorders. Tight junctions form the core structure of the selective permeability barrier between intestinal epithelial cells, consisting of tight junction proteins, including transmembrane components such as Claudin-1 and Occludin, and peripheral membrane-associated scaffold proteins such as ZO-1. Tight junction proteins create highly organized intercellular contacts through tight adhesion. The disruption or loss of them leads to increased intestinal mucosal permeability, allowing the passage of pathogenic microorganisms and harmful substances, thereby triggering and exacerbating intestinal inflammation. The data from this study demonstrated that fluoride exposure significantly elevated the blood levels of D-LA and DAO, resulting in increased intestinal epithelial permeability in mice. The mRNA expression and protein levels of the three tight junction proteins further confirmed the impairment of the intestinal barrier function in mice. Exposure to fluoride-containing drinking water has been shown to impair intestinal development across multiple segments and to suppress tight junction protein expression, thereby increasing mucosal permeability. Among the segments of the intestine, the ileum appears to experience the greatest adverse effects when exposed to fluoride. Administration of GY007 at 1 x 109 CFU ameliorated the fluoride-induced increase in intestinal epithelial permeability, providing a robust basis for restoring intestinal barrier function.

Our recent study employed single-cell sequencing technology to investigate fluoride-induced damage to the ileum. The results showed that the expression of Duox2 and Duoxa2 in the ileal cells of fluoride-exposed mice was elevated, and the level of 4-HNE also increased. Consistent with these observations, this study found that oxidative stress levels in the ileal tissues of mice exposed to a high fluoride exposure were elevated. Duox2 is an epithelial antimicrobial dual oxidase, with Duoxa2 serving as a key maturation factor for the enzyme. MacFie et al. have reported that in individuals experiencing active ulcerative colitis, the mature Duox2-Duoxa2 complex is the main enzyme system that generates reactive oxygen species (specifically hydrogen peroxide). Administration of GY007 permits the targeted modulation of these indices. Fluoride treatment decreased intestinal SOD and CAT and increased MDA in mice, which has been observed in both rat and chicken models. Notably, fluoride exposure did not elicit a significant alteration in ileal glutathione (GSH) levels in the present study. This finding suggested that fluoride may exert a distinct pattern of oxidative stress injury in the ileum; however, additional evidence is required to substantiate this conclusion. While GY007 exhibited a partial reduction in H2O2 levels, its ability to fully alleviate oxidative stress remains limited, and further optimization of the GY007 administration protocol may enhance its efficacy. These findings suggest that GY007 could partially alleviate oxidative stress damage in the ileum of mice caused by fluoride exposure, but further research is required to fully assess its potential.

Notably, some findings in this study differ from prior reports, particularly regarding Reg3b/Reg3g and ileal Bifidobacterium abundance. Previous work reported increased Reg3b/Reg3g expression and higher MUC2 and Ramp1 abundance in the ileum after chronic fluoride exposure, where a mouse model was exposed to drinking water fluoride at a concentration of 25/50 ppm for a duration of 56 weeks, whereas Reg3b/Reg3g showed an opposite trend in our gavage model (24 mg/kg NaF for 8 weeks). Fluoride exposure reduced ileal Bifidobacterium in the present study, whereas our earlier work in ICR mice using fluoride exposure via drinking water for 10 weeks showed an increase. This discrepancy may be attributable to differences in the experimental animal, fluoride exposure paradigms, including the route of administration, and the duration of treatment. Reg3 proteins are thought to contribute to restoration and repair processes within the intestinal mucosa. It exhibits antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activities, supports tissue regeneration, and contributes to the maintenance of intestinal homeostasis. One study reported that mice lacking Reg3b exhibited exacerbated colitis manifestations relative to their wild-type counterparts. The MUC2 gene encodes the predominant secreted mucin in the intestinal tract, constituting a major structural component of the mucus layer and acting as a critical contributor in protecting the ileal mucosa from infectious challenges. When Ramp1 is lacking, animals exhibit heightened epithelial stress and become more vulnerable to infection by pathogenic bacteria. Overall, our observations indicated that fluoride exposure disrupts intestinal mucosal homeostasis. Treatment with GY007 significantly reversed the changes in the indicators associated with ileal mucosal dysfunction induced by fluoride. The distinct Reg3a expression pattern may suggest a different regulatory response to GY007, which warrants further investigation. Future studies should investigate how GY007 modulates the regenerating gene family dynamics within the murine small intestine subjected to long-term fluoride exposure via drinking water. Elucidating whether the probiotic responses are tuned to specific physiological processes will provide a rationale for targeted investigations into probiotic engraftment and accumulation.

Increased intestinal permeability can activate pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, thereby contributing to the development of intestinal inflammation. Consistent with this, fluoride exposure within this investigation increased ileal mRNA levels of TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IFN-alpha, whereas GY007 administration significantly downregulated the expression of pro-inflammatory mediators. Accumulating evidence indicates that probiotics can modulate inflammatory mediators. One study reported that a combined probiotic formulation comprising Clostridium butyricum and Bifidobacterium infantis ameliorated intestinal injury by normalizing IFN-gamma, IL-10, and TNF-alpha levels. Streptococcus thermophiles mitigated inflammatory responses by lowering TNF-alpha and enhancing IFN-gamma and IL-10. Notably, fluoride exposure in the present study did not significantly alter IL-10 or IFN-gamma levels. Although GY007 tended to attenuate the fluoride-associated increase in IL-17, this effect did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.062). TNF-alpha, IL-6, and IFN-alpha are downstream inflammatory mediators of Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling (Figure S1). TLRs are pattern recognition receptors and are essential mediators of immune activity at mucosal surfaces. Further detection of the key mediators on the TLR pathway revealed that fluoride significantly increased the levels of IRF7, IRAK4, Myd88, and NF-kappab, while GY007 could reverse this trend. During the process of fluoride damage, only TLR9 and TLR4 showed significant changes, while GY007 only had an effect on TLR9. Situated within endosomal compartments, TLR9 acts as a specialized DNA sensor by detecting CpG dinucleotide motifs that are unmethylated or only minimally methylated, including those in immune complexes, and subsequently leads to the engagement of Myd88. As a pivotal adaptor in the TLR9 signaling cascade, Myd88 facilitates NF-kappab phosphorylation and activation by recruiting members of the interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase (IRAK) family. Upon activation, NF-kappab translocates to the cell nucleus, where it induces the transcription of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines and co-stimulatory molecules, culminating in tissue injury. Overall, these data suggest that the key components of the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway may be involved in the modulation of immune homeostasis in the ileum of mice by the intervention with GY007. Future investigations should conduct further research in relevant areas to clarify the mechanism of the effects of probiotics.

The small intestine not only acts as a barrier but also provides a living environment for microorganisms. On the basis of the AB/PAS staining results, we subsequently performed a more detailed analysis of the intestinal microbial community. The findings indicated that probiotic intervention restored fluoride-disrupted gut microbiota diversity, as shown by the rebound in the reduced Simpson and Shannon indices and the normalization of community composition and structure. We conducted a comparative analysis between groups to further assess the variation in Bifidobacterium levels across the different treatment cohorts. Notably, both LEfSe and machine learning analyses identified Bifidobacterium as a discriminative biomarker; moreover, it exhibited the highest feature importance score in the machine learning model, further underscoring the role of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. animalis GY007 in modulating and maintaining gut microbial homeostasis. Administration of GY007 was associated with an enrichment of intestinal Bifidobacterium and Dubosiella, accompanied by a decrease in Paramuribaculum and Kineothrix et al. Bifidobacteria are well-established probiotics recognized for their beneficial effects on gut health. Compared with Akkermansia muciniphila, Dubosiella has been reported to exhibit stronger probiotic efficacy, providing greater protection against colonic mucosal barrier injury and attenuating intestinal inflammation. Kineothrix is positively correlated with intestinal inflammation, while Paramuribaculum is regarded as a potential pathogenic bacterium associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). GY007 may facilitate intestinal repair by modulating the microbiota environment, as reflected by the enrichment of advantageous taxa alongside a decline in potentially pathogenic bacterial groups.

The untargeted metabolomics analysis identified a total of 48 metabolites present in both comparisons. For example, the F group showed elevated levels of HIA and ISO, whereas both metabolites were markedly lower in the F+Bi group; conversely, GLA, SAB, and SIA were diminished under fluoride exposure but became significantly more abundant following administration with GY007. HIA is a benzoic acid-related compound and ranks among the predominant organic acids detected in mammalian urine, functioning as an important co-metabolite that links microbial activity in the gut with host metabolism. Ni et al. demonstrated that the gut microbiota-mediated and host-dependent accumulation of hippuric acid results in an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. Evidence from both animal models and cell-based systems indicates that GLA contributes to preserving gut homeostasis while regulating the abundance of proteins involved in tight junction architecture, cell adhesion, and focal adhesion assemblies. The selection of ISO (MP3188), OIC-7alpha (MN18722), and SIA (MP9998) was based on their observed correlations with multiple ileal injury indicators across the experimental groups. ISO, a nucleobase derivative, may reflect altered microbial nucleotide metabolism, while OIC-7alpha, a bile acid biosynthesis intermediate, is implicated in regulating intestinal barrier integrity and inflammation pathways through receptors like FXR. SIA, a phenolic compound, is known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, which contribute to reducing intestinal inflammation. Furthermore, we performed KEGG pathway analysis on the metabolites showing differential abundance. The histidine metabolism signaling pathway was simultaneously observed in both the Ctrl vs. F comparison and the F vs. F+Bi comparison, and it holds significant importance. The metabolic process of histidine (HIS) is closely associated with the intestinal microbial community and appears to be an important determinant of the onset and worsening of chronic disorders. Among human proteins, HIS contains the smallest proportion of essential amino acids. Variations in its abundance, as well as exogenous supplementation, have been linked to multiple potential health-promoting effects, notably antioxidant activity and attenuation of inflammatory responses. However, excessive intake of HIS may elicit detrimental outcomes, including cell apoptosis and increased tissue damage. This indicated the importance of maintaining a stable state rather than simply increasing or decreasing the levels of substances. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the combined indicators of the microbial community, metabolic community, and intestinal function. There were correlations between the microbial community, metabolic community and the intestinal function indicators after the GY007 intervention. Further detailed analysis revealed that the Bifidobacterium was associated with each of these indicators. Among the several metabolites of concern, the prioritized metabolites, ISO, OIC 7alpha, and SIA, emphasized the integrative metabolic shifts that may explain the therapeutic effects of GY007 in alleviating fluoride-induced damage. The above results further demonstrate the significance of the Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. animalis GY007 and the substances that we need to pay attention to particularly.

Although this study has demonstrated the therapeutic efficacy of GY007 in alleviating fluoride-induced ileal injury, certain limitations remain. Firstly, the analysis was limited to the ileum, a specific segment of the intestine, and therefore the findings may not be generalizable to the entire gastrointestinal system. Additional studies are warranted to evaluate the impact of GY007 on other regions of the intestine. Secondly, although the 24 mg/kg body weight dosage of sodium fluoride over 8 weeks induced significant toxic effects on the murine ileum in the present study, future research should include preliminary toxicity assessments of sodium fluoride following established toxicity guidelines. Thirdly, additional investigation is required to clarify whether GY007 alleviates damage to the ileum through a primary mechanism acting on the tissue itself, or instead via secondary pathways that mediate the observed protective outcome. This could be explored through future experiments involving antibiotic-induced perturbation of the gut microbiota.

passages.text: 5. Conclusions

The investigation demonstrated that B. animalis subsp. animalis GY007 as a potential probiotic strain could mitigate the ileal injury and restore the microbiota-metabolite balance disrupted by high fluoride exposure. Its principal functions include maintaining the integrity of the ileal epithelial barrier and associated mucosal functions, modulating antioxidant capacity, and influencing inflammatory mediators potentially linked to the TLR9/NF-kappab/IRF7 signaling pathway, as well as restoring the dysbiosis of both the microbiota and metabolome. Microbial analysis further highlighted the role of Bifidobacterium animalis in this process. Metabolic analysis identified ISO, OIC-7alpha, and SIA as key metabolites (Figure 10). However, the underlying mechanism remains incompletely understood, and further studies are needed to explore this aspect. Future work should employ causality-oriented approaches, such as targeted microbiota/metabolite depletion or modulation. In summary, this research identified a probiotic that could mitigate ileal injury caused by high fluoride exposure, providing valuable insights for developing therapeutic strategies to alleviate the biological harm associated with environmental fluoride pollution. Moreover, our findings offer an integrative perspective on microbiota-host interactions in the context of fluoride exposure.

passages.text: Genomic estimates of Identity-By-Descent relationships in large scale data sets
Background

Genomic relationship and inbreeding estimates are either based on genetic drift (e.g. the Genomic Relationship Matrix; GRM), homozygosity (e.g. Runs of Homozygosity; ROH), or Identity-By-Descent (IBD). A genomic IBD-based relationship matrix, Gla, is obtained by linkage analysis which uses genomic data to distinguish paternal versus maternal inheritances of chromosomal segments to replace the 50/50 probabilities used to calculate pedigree-based relationships (A matrix). Our aim was to develop a fast approximate algorithm, FGla, to estimate the Gla matrix in large complex pedigrees making use of dense marker genotypes, and to compare Gla to A, GRM and ROH based inbreeding (FROH) in simulated and a large scale Norwegian Red Cattle (NRF) data set.
Results

Given pedigree data and >= 3 generations of 45 k marker genotypes, marker positions were detected that unambiguously identified maternal/paternal inheritance, and inheritances at intermediate positions were imputed by the Viterbi algorithm from the positions with known inheritance. Any remaining unknown inheritances were randomly sampled (paternal or maternal), and the sampling errors that this introduced were averaged out by the large number of marker loci used (correlation between replicated estimates: 0.9998). Also, calculations were limited to the relationship coefficients that were actually needed, assuming that relationships for a limited set of candidates were needed. The accuracy of estimated Gla coefficients increased from 0.971 to 0.998, when genotyping increased from the actually genotyped NRF cattle towards all pedigreed animals. The accuracy of the GRM was 0.936, but required only genotyping of the animals whose relationships were needed. Gla relationships were approximately unbiased in the Best Linear Unbiased Prediction (BLUP) sense. Hence, if Gla based inbreeding management predicts an increase in relationships then an identical increase in true IBD relationships is expected. Gla uses the same base population as A, namely that of the pedigree.
Conclusions

An approximate computationally efficient multipoint linkage analysis algorithm was developed to estimate unbiased IBD-based relationship and inbreeding coefficients. Its unbiasedness and precise definition of the base population makes it well suited for the genomic management of inbreeding and genomic optimal contribution selection. In addition, Gla based optimal contribution selection is neutral with respect to allele frequency changes.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12711-026-01038-9.
Background

Genomic relationships and/or inbreeding estimates are based on (i) homozygosity, i.e. Identity by State (IBS), (ii) genetic drift and/or (iii) Identity by Descent (IBD) expressed relative to a (recent) base population. Homozygosity can be single locus based, e.g. excess of homozygosity, or Runs of Homozygosity (ROHs), i.e. homozygosity of marker haplotypes. In case of (i), inbreeding is based on homozygosity at loci on the two homologous chromosomes, and molecular coancestry of a pair of individuals is based on the average homozygosity when comparing the sets of homologous chromosomes pairwise, resulting in a 2 x 2 table of comparisons. Although ROHs are strictly homozygous haplotypes, the concept of ROHs is based on extensive runs of homozygosity, which are unlikely to occur by chance, implying that ROHs have a high probability of being IBD. Hence, ROHs combine information sources (i) and (iii).

For information source (ii), VanRaden's genomic relationship matrix (GRM) measures relationship and inbreeding as the (co)variances of allele frequency changes relative to reference allele frequencies. Pedigree based inbreeding is based on loops in the pedigree, and so are pedigree relationship matrices (A), since IBD relationships between a pair of animals result in inbreeding in their (putative) offspring, implying source (iii). Utilizing genomic data, linkage analysis may be used to assess the inheritances (paternal or maternal) at any locus j and thus to assess IBD versus non-IBD, resulting in an IBD based relationship matrix at locus j. Averaging this IBD matrix over all loci results in an overall IBD based relationship matrix called Gla. The latter is however computationally very challenging as a linkage analysis at a single locus is demanding in large complex pedigrees, especially when many genotypes are missing. Parallel computations may alleviate this problem, but building many local IBD relationship matrices simultaneously requires large amounts of computer memory. Also, since Gla equals the mean of all  across all loci j, it cannot be easily inverted, unlike A or the single-locus  matrix.

While these computational costs can be significant, they are offset by the potential to approximate true IBD relationships, if paternal or maternal inheritances that occur in the pedigree and along the genomes are (partly) identified by marker data. Hence, instead of the 50/50 segregation probabilities that are used to construct the A-matrix, the actual paternal or maternal inheritances may be identified by tracing the inheritance of marker alleles through the pedigree using linkage analysis. If a marker locus is not informative, e.g. the parent was homozygous, other adjacent loci may be used to infer paternal/maternal inheritance. With 50 k SNPs and a 3000 cM genome, there are ~ 17 SNPs per cM, and if two adjacent markers < 1 cM away indicate e.g. paternal inheritance, the probability of paternal inheritance at the locus of interest is close to 100%. Hence, an IBD matrix may be set up that resembles the true IBD matrix closely, if all animals are genotyped. However, if some animals are not genotyped, we will have to rely on the A-matrix assumption of 50/50 segregation probabilities for these undetermined inheritances, and the Gla matrix will increasingly resemble A as the number of ungenotyped animals increases.

An advantage of IBD relationships versus IBS is that if a segment is IBD then all loci on this segment are expected to be identical (except for mutations). The latter is useful for inferences on non-genotyped loci, QTL mapping, and genome-wide inferences of inbreeding. Also, for the genomic management of genetic variation by optimal contribution selection (OCS), the use of IBD relationships has been proposed because directly restricting the rate of increase of homozygosity at marker loci resulted in excessive genetic drift, and directly restricting the rate of increase of GRM relationships resulted in excessive loss of heterozygosity. Our aim is here to develop a fast approximate algorithm to set up the Gla matrix, called FGla, in large complex pedigrees making use of dense marker genotypes. For reasons of computational efficiency, FGla does not perform a full multilocus linkage analysis, as LDMIP does, but only uses information from neighbouring loci when these are informative about the paternal/maternal inheritance at a particular locus. We will compare the Gla matrix to A, GRM, and ROH based inbreeding estimates and Gla, A, and GRM relationship estimates in simulated data and in a large dairy cattle data set.
Methods
Estimating Gla

Fernando and Grossman adapted the tabular method for the calculation of A matrix relationships towards a method to calculate the (2Nx2N) linkage analysis based gametic relationship matrix at position j, where N is the number of animals in the pedigree and every animal has two entries, one for its paternal and one for its maternal gamete. Fernando and Grossman's algorithm requires that the pedigreed individuals are consecutively numbered 1,2,3,..,N from old to young individuals, i.e. parents precede their offspring, which is also assumed in the current algorithm. The gametic relationship matrix may be condensed into the (N x N)  matrix by summing the 4 elements belonging to a pair of animals and dividing this sum by 2. In the current setting, this requires the calculation of an NxN matrix at M positions, where M is the number of SNPs on the SNP-chip (e.g. M = 50 k). We will assume that not all NxN relationships amongst all pedigreed individuals are needed, but only the relationships amongst a limited set of n 'candidates' called C are needed, and n <  < N. E.g. in OCS, C is the set of selection candidates. We will thus calculate the (n x n) IBD relationships for the set C of individuals for all positions j = 1,..,M.

Workflow of the FGla algorithm. a for some genotyped individuals at some loci the paternal or maternal allele can be identified (in italics) and the segregation indicator is identified (maternal inheritance indicated in red here). b Segregation indicators in between the known indicators are imputed by the Viterbi algorithm (indicated by _) and others are randomly sampled (indicated in blue). c Allocating unique founder alleles to the founders of the pedigree and following the known segregation indicators yields founder alleles for all individuals. The last individual is inbred at the B locus since it carries the same founder allele: B9

In the following, we will first, based on the marker data, identify the (2NxM) matrix of segregation indicators S, i.e. determine for each gamete at each locus whether the paternal or maternal allele of its parent was inherited. Every individual has two rows of segregation indicators in S: one for its paternally and one for its maternally inherited chromosome. Next, we will calculate the n(n + 1)/2 lower triangle of elements of . In order to reduce computer memory requirements, the  matrices are not explicitly set up. Instead, for any of the n(n + 1)/2 required elements, say (i,k), we will calculate  for all loci j, and take the average over the loci to arrive at . The calculation of the n(n + 1)/2 required elements of  is performed in parallel on the same node, whereas different chromosomes may be calculated in parallel on different computer nodes. The workflow of the algorithm is outlined in Fig. 1.
Segregation indicators S

The segregation indicators, S, are 1, 2, or 0 indicating paternal, maternal or unknown inheritance. For example, if  and if i is even, this indicates that the gamete that individual i/2 inherited from its mother is a copy of the mother's paternal (maternal) allele at locus j. We also define P: a (2N x M) matrix indicating whether a heterozygous genotype is sorted or not (1 or 0), where sorted means that we distinguish between '12' and'21' genotypes where e.g. '21' implies that the '2' allele was inherited from its father (both alleles pertaining to the sorted heterozygous genotype will be set to 1 in P). Since S and P can only be non-zero for genotyped individuals, their storage requirement is limited to the genotyped individuals. The following algorithm calculates first the segregation indicators at positions where the marker genotypes are informative about, and next interpolates from these positions to the adjacent loci at gamete i, as also implemented in many common phasing algorithms:
Step 0: Set all .
Step 1: Find parent - offspring pairs where both are genotyped.

Step 2: Find all loci where the offspring is heterozygous and its parent is homozygous, which implies that we know which of the offsprings alleles came from this parent (since the parent transmitted only one possible allele). If the other parent is also genotyped, check for Mendelian consistency, i.e. two identical homozygous parental genotypes cannot produce a heterozygous offspring. In case of Mendelian consistency, sort the offspring's heterozygous genotypes as '12' or '21' depending on the paternal/maternal inheritance and set  for the offspring's gametes; in case of a Mendelian inconsistency, the heterozygote is considered unsorted .

Step 3: Again in genotyped parent-offspring pairs, find loci where the parent has a sorted heterozygous genotype (whose gametes have ), and its offspring is homozygous, which implies that we know which allele was inherited from the parent (namely the allele for which the offspring is homozygous), and since  we know whether this is the paternal or maternal allele. If the paternal (maternal) allele was inherited: set .

Step 4: For the imputation of the missing  values in between (and next to) known  values, a Hidden Markov Model was applied to each chromosome with some known and unknown . In particular, the Viterbi algorithm was used to find the most likely mosaic of paternal and maternal inheritances (2 hidden states) across the chromosome where recombinations from paternal to maternal state and vice versa are modelled as state transitions. The hidden states were matched against the observed  values from Step 3 allowing for an error (in any of the Steps 1-3) probability of 0.05. This error rate allows for genotyping errors in any of the three genotyped generations and for possible marker map errors, which could induce erroneous recombination events. The recombination rate was assumed equal to the average distance between the loci in base pairs times 10-8. The Viterbi algorithm finds the most likely path, i.e. pattern of paternal and maternal inheritances, along the chromosome, which yields the  values for gamete i and for all loci j (see Additional file 1 Text S1 for details on the implementation of the Viterbi algorithm). It may be noted that Steps 2 and 3 require at least 3 consecutive generations of genotypes, i.e. homozygous grandparents, heterozygous parents (with sorted genotypes), and homozygous offspring.
Allocation of founder alleles given known

At each locus j, unique founder alleles will be allocated to each gamete of the base animals of the pedigree, i.e. the founder alleles of the base animals are coded 1,...,2Nbase, where Nbase is the number of base animals of the pedigree (animals with unknown parents). If all  are known, this would determine the inheritance of these founder alleles through the entire pedigree. Moreover, if a descendant inherits from both its parents the same founder allele code at locus j, then both alleles are a copy of the same unique base population allele, and the descendant is thus inbred at locus j, i.e. identity of founder loci directly indicates IBD.

Where , i.e. unknown, we sampled either paternal or maternal inheritance, with 50/50 probability, as in the gene-dropping method. This introduces sampling errors on the estimates of  at position j, but we expect this sampling error to average out over many independently evaluated marker loci j resulting in a small overall sampling error over many (here 45 k) positions. This averaging out of the sampled  coefficients over many samples to estimate relationship estimates was also proposed in the gene-dropping algorithm. Furthermore, sampling errors are reduced by sampling the  coefficients independently from samples at other positions, although this is not the case in real data. The independent sampling of  results in unbiased estimates of  at each position j, and thus also in an unbiased estimate of its average: .

Instead of gene-dropping all founder alleles through the entire pedigree, we concentrated on assessing the inherited founder alleles for the required candidates set C of size n. To achieve this we applied the following algorithm at every locus j:
Step 0: Let FAj be a vector of founder allele IDs of size 2N at position j, and initialise FAj to the unique founder alleles 1,..,2Nbase, for the base animals, and to zeros for non-founder alleles.
For each allele i of each individual in the set C of required animals:
Step 1a: If FAj(i)=0 (founder allele is unknown) initialise a list of IDs of i and its ancestors ANC, i.e. set ANC=[i], and set the current ancestor gamete k=i:
Step 1b: let k' be the parental gamete of k, which is determined by the pedigree of the animal carrying k and its segregation indicator Skj. If Skj=0, its value is sampled (1 or 2).
Step 1c: if FAj[k']>0, the founder allele is identified and set equal to IDFA=FAj[k'] and continue with Step 2; else: add k' to the ancestor list ANC, set k = k', and return to Step 1b.
Step 2: set FAj for all alleles in the ANC list to IDFA, i.e. FAj(ANC)=IDFA.
End and return the vector of founder alleles at position j: FAj.

This algorithm is applied to each locus j independently. We did not attempt to parallelise this algorithm which allocates founder alleles to all animals in the set C (and as a byproduct: the founder alleles of the ancestors of the set C animals).
Calculation of Gla
Given the founder alleles FAj, we calculate the inbreeding coefficient averaged over all positions j for each animal i of set C with paternal (maternal) gamete i' (i'') as:

We performed the calculation of  on a per chromosome basis, so that different chromosomes could be processed by different computer nodes. In order, to obtain the genome-wide  matrix, we averaged the chromosome-wise  matrices weighted by their number of SNPs. Julia scripts for the calculation of the segregation indicators and  matrix are available from a GitHub repository (github.com/theomeuwissen/FGla).
Data sets: simulated and real

We used the FGla algorithm to estimate the  matrix of a set of 10,311 Norwegian Red cows (NRC) that were genotyped and born in 2022, which represents the target set C and may reflect a typical candidate population for optimal contribution selection. Geno (www.geno.no) kindly provided a pedigree of these cows with 393,129 entries. The average depth of the pedigree of the 10,311 cows was 8 generations. Within this set of 10,311 cows, it was on average 3.9 generations ago since a non-genotyped ancestor occurred (averaged over the ancestral lineages). Geno also provided SNP chip genotypes for 44,754 SNPs, with a minor allele frequency > 0.01, on 141,977 individuals, which includes the 10,311 cows and as many as possible of their genotyped ancestors. This real data set is called Real(NRC).

passages.text: Since true IBD is unknown in real data, we performed also computer simulations that mimicked the real data, called Sim(NRC). Genotypes for the base animals of the pedigree were randomly sampled from the real available phased genotypes. These genotypes were gene-dropped down the real pedigree of the cows, where at random either the paternal or maternal alleles were inherited at the beginning of each chromosome, and the inheritance swapped each time a recombination occurred along the chromosome. The number of recombinations was sampled from a Poisson distribution with mean equal to the size of the chromosome measured in 100 mega-base units, i.e. 10-8 recombinations per base pair. The sampled number of recombinations were randomly positioned along the chromosome without interference. The simulated paternal/maternal inheritances at the SNP positions were used to calculate the true IBD matrix of the 10,311 cows (IBD). The genotypes of the base animals were gene-dropped along the chromosomes through the pedigree using the paternal/maternal inheritance patterns described above, but in data set Sim(NRC) only the genotypes of the 141,977 animals that were actually genotyped in the real data were available for analysis. To investigate the effect of increased genotyping efforts that would help to identify segregation indicators, also the data set Sim(NRC + PGP) was simulated, where in addition to the actually genotyped animals all the parents and grand-parents of the 10,311 set C animals were assumed genotyped, which increased the number of genotyped animals to 153,143. Furthermore, in order to investigate the effect of genotyping all pedigreed animals, data set Sim(All) was simulated where all animals in the pedigree were genotyped, i.e. 393,129 genotyped individuals. The simulated data sets were replicated tenfold, and the sizes of all these data sets are summarized in Table 1.
Comparison of methods

Next to  and IBD (for simulated data), also the pedigree relationship matrix A, and the Genomic Relationship Matrix (GRM) were compared for the 10,311 cows. The GRM was calculated as:where  is an (n x M) matrix of centred genotype codes:  for homozygote, heterozygote and alternative homozygote genotypes, respectively; and  is the allele frequency in the base population of the pedigree. For the simulated data sets, base population allele frequencies were known. For the Real(NRC) data, base population allele frequencies were estimated as , where  is a vector of non-centred genotypes coded 0, 1 or 2 for SNP j, and  is the pedigree relationship matrix of the 141,977 genotyped animals.

Inbreeding coefficients were obtained from the diagonals of these relationship matrices minus 1. We also used runs of homozygosity to calculate inbreeding (FROH). FROH was calculated for the 10,311 cows using Plink, with a minimum ROH length of 2 Mb and 30 SNPs per ROH, a minimum density of 75 kb per SNP, and default Plink settings for the remaining parameters. The expected coalescence time of 2 Mb segments is 25 generations, i.e. FROH is expected to trace inbreeding up to 25 generations ago, although coalescence times are very variable (they have an exponential distribution with a coefficient of variation of 100%), which implies that also older and younger ancestors are expected to contribute significantly to ROHs of 2 Mb.

Analyses of the simulated data

The information content of the genotyped data for the estimation of Gla relationships may be measured by (1) the fraction of the gametes for which (some) segregation indicators were determined by the genotypes Fr(#S > 0); and (2) the fraction of SNPs with determined segregation indicators given that > 0 indicators were determined on the gamete Fr(#S/M l #S > 0). Fr(#S > 0) was 0.234, 0.267, and 0.769 for the data sets Sim(NRC), Sim(NRC + PGP), and Sim(All), respectively. As expected, Fr(#S > 0) increases with the number of genotyped animals, but remains < 1 even if all animals are genotyped, because the base animals and their offspring do not have 3 generations of genotyped ancestors. Also, the asymmetry of the pedigree (more unknown dams than sires) may have reduced Fr(#S > 0). Fr(#S/M l #S > 0) was 0.163, 0.173 and 0.229 for Sim(NRC), Sim(NRC + PGP), and Sim(All), respectively, which increases somewhat with the number of genotyped animals because the probability that both grand-parents are genotyped increases. For Sim(NRC), Fr(#S/M l #S > 0) = 0.163 implies that ~ 3 informative SNPs per megabase are used by the Viterbi algorithm to impute the missing segregation indicators. Generally, it is expected that Fr(#S/M l #S > 0) increases with the information content of the markers, in particular as their heterozygosity increases.

Analyses of the real (NRC) data

The average inbreeding and relationships of the NRC cows were approximately 0.014 and 0.04, respectively, for both Gla and A, and were substantially higher for the GRM (Table 4). The latter is contrary to expectations based on the simulations of Table 1, but may be explained by the use of estimated base population allele frequencies instead of true frequencies, which were used in the simulations. The estimation errors on the base population allele frequency estimates inflate GRM inbreeding and relationships estimates since they imply additional drift of allele frequencies, which inflates the GRM's drift-based inbreeding and relationship estimates. The average FROH is substantially larger at 0.0746 than expected based on the simulations (0.0453), which may imply that FROH traces some relationships that occurred before the other methods' base populations.

This model assumes thus that genomic relationships deviate from pedigree relationships by Mendelian samplings and/or by sampling of a finite number of SNPs. Thus, the model implies that the covariance of pedigree and genomic relationships equals the variance of the pedigree relationships, because no covariance is expected between the pedigree relationships and the residuals due to Mendelian and/or SNP sampling. The latter implies a regression coefficient of genomic on pedigree relationships/inbreeding of 1, which is approximately observed for Gla relationships. For GRM inbreeding coefficients b < 1, which may be because Geno uses GRM relationships in mating decisions, which reduces their variance and covariance with pedigree relationships.
Computational costs

Since on multi-node computer systems the calculations of different chromosomes can be distributed over different nodes and thus can be performed in parallel, we report here the computational costs for the Real(NRC) data of chromosome BTA15, which is an average-sized chromosome with 1488 SNPs and ~ 84 cM. The calculation of the segregation indicators and parallelised calculation of the 53,163,516 (= 10,311*(10,311 + 1)/2) relationship coefficients cost ~ 15 min wall clock time, ~ 74 min CPU time and was performed by on average 5 CPU cores on an AMD 3970X 32-Core Processor. Maximum RAM memory requirements were 12.4 GB.
Discussion

An approximate linkage analysis method, called FGla, was developed to calculate genomic relationship and inbreeding coefficients in large scale practical data sets. The method was applied to a practical NRC data set consisting of ~ 45 k SNPs and a target population of ~ 10 k (selection) candidates, and a simulated population of similar size. Unlike alternative genomic measures of relationship and inbreeding, linkage analysis makes use of pedigree data for the estimation of relationships among genotyped animals, and the current pedigree contained 393 k animals of which 142 k were genotyped. The efficiency of the relationship calculations were enhanced by (1) restricting them to a limited sized target population whose relationships were actually needed instead of calculating the entire 393 k x 393 k relationship matrix of all pedigreed animals; (2) leveraging high density marker genotypes by using informative marker positions to calculate unambiguous segregation indicators that were either paternal or maternal and interpolating the missing segregation indicators; and (3) independently sampling any missing segregation indicators (50/50) and relying on the large numbers of markers to average out sampling errors. If the latter is not the case, e.g. because Gla is needed for a small chromosomal segment, Gla may be calculated multiple times and averaged in order to average out the sampling errors. Although approximate and based on 45 k SNP-chip data, the accuracy of the Gla matrix estimates may be as high as 0.998 and 0.986 for relationship and inbreeding coefficients, respectively, when all animals were genotyped (Table 3). These results on simulated and real NRC data are illustrative rather than generalizable. To determine the full utility of FGla, more work on populations with different/no inbreeding management, and showing different patterns of missing genotypes will be needed.

In a practical NRC data set, per chromosome computing costs were moderate at about 15 min of wall-clock time on a multi-core processor for the calculation of the segregation indicators and Gla, respectively, and multiple computer nodes can process many chromosomes in parallel. Computations are expected to increase quadratically with the number of relationship coefficients required, and linearly if we only need inbreeding coefficients. The size of the pedigree is expected to increase computations linearly, and also the number of SNPs will increase computations linearly.

Marker positions, that unambiguously indicated the segregation indicators, were used to identify segregation indicators, and missing indicators were imputed for other marker positions on the chromosome using the Viterbi algorithm. Higher SNP densities are expected to improve the accuracy of this interpolation. Since haplotypes are more frequently heterozygous than individual SNPs, their use would increase the information content of the genotypes, but this would require phased genotypes and switch errors of the phasing may be interpreted as recombinations by the segregation indicator estimation algorithm. However, since the correlation of Gla with true IBD coefficients is very high at 0.998 (Table 3) when all animals are genotyped, this increase in accuracy by increasing SNP density beyond ~ 15 k SNPs/Gb (= 45 k / 3 Gb genome) is expected to be limited.

The Gla, A, GRM and IBD relationships all use the same base population, which is the founder population of the pedigree, i.e. the animals with unknown parents, which are assumed unrelated and non-inbred. In the simulated data, GRM relationships equalled on average those of Gla, A and IBD, but for the real data they were increased probably due to estimation errors on the base population allele frequencies. For FROH, the base population is not well defined although it is expected to be approximately 1/(2c) generations ago, where c is the minimum ROH length in Morgans. The latter is here ~ 0.02 M implying a base population ~ 25 generations ago, but variances on these estimates are high such that older and younger ancestors are expected to contribute significantly to these ROHs of 0.02 M. The average depth of the pedigree was 8 generations, which may explain why Froh is generally higher than Fped and more variable.

The finding that the regressions of IBD on Gla (and A) relationships are close to 1, is important for inbreeding management, since this implies that an expected increase in relationships of, say, 1% based on Gla, results in an actual increase in IBD relationships of 1%. Furthermore this finding implies that Gla and A yield approximately unbiased estimators of IBD in the sense that E[IBDl Gla]   Gla, which is the BLUP sense of unbiasedness.

In addition, the Gla is expected to be semi-positive definite, i.e. has eigenvalues >= 0, which is an important property for OCS, because otherwise the group coancestry of a set of selected parents, , may be negative for some parental contributions c, even though the coancestries are based on IBD probabilities and thus should be between 0 and 1. At any locus j,  relationships are based on the (non)-identity of founder alleles, hence, if the founder allele's effects are assumed independent and identically distributed with variance 1,  yields the (co)variance matrix of these allelic effects at locus j, and (co)variance matrices are by definition semi-positive definite.  is the average of many , which is thus also a (co)variance matrix and semi-positive definite. The GRM is also semi-positive definite since it is the (co)variance matrix of marker alleles.

Although not attempted here, ROHs may also be used to calculate relationships between individuals. This requires phased genotype data, and such ROHs may thus be affected by phasing errors. These ROH calculations are required for each of the (2 x 2) = 4 combinations of gametes of each pair of individuals, which would require ~ 212 million genome-wide FROH calculations for the current set of 10,311 candidates. HapIBD can perform rapid ROH calculations across many pairs of individuals, but offers limited flexibility in defining ROHs. Also, because ROH-based relationship calculations are performed on a one pair at a time basis, it is not clear, when put together, they form a consistent ROH-based relationship matrix, i.e. whether the resulting matrix will be (semi-) positive definite. However inconsistent matrices may be 'bended' to become positive definite (see e.g.).

Since the FGla method uses only marker data at positions where the markers are informative about the paternal/maternal inheritances, FGla readily handles any occasional missing genotypes, which are treated the same as non-informative genotypes. Also, non-genotyped animals (or animals whose genotypes are non-informative because their parents are not genotyped) are readily handled by sampling their segregation indicators, which averaged over many loci results in the gene-dropping based estimates of relationship. Hence, Gla is a genomic relationship matrix that combines genotyped and non-genotyped animals, i.e. Gla forms a consistent relationship matrix for genotyped and ungenotyped animals. This property is important when including some ungenotyped selection candidates in OCS, and Gla shares this property with the H matrix from the single step genomic selection literature.

For genomic inbreeding management (GOCS), the use of IBD based relationships, such as Gla, was recommended, because drift-based relationships, such as in the GRM, resulted in increased losses of rare alleles, and homozygosity-based relationships, e.g. measured by ROHs, resulted in increased genetic drift. This recommendation was based on a simulation study of 10 chromosomes of 100 cM each, whereas the cattle, pig, sheep and salmon genomes are about 3 times this size, and the poultry genome is about twice the size. Comparing the results of our simulations of BTA15 with those of 29 chromosomes clearly showed that with many chromosomes relationships estimates become closer to their expectation based on the pedigree A, i.e. when more loci are sampled the resulting paternal/maternal proportions are closer to their 50/50 expectation. Also, assuming no selection, the expectation of the GRM equals A, when many (unlinked) positions are evaluated. This suggests that the differences between the alternative matrices on genetic drift and loss of heterozygosity are expected to be smaller in practical GOCS schemes for species with large genomes. GOCS results using GRM or IBD based relationship matrices are also more similar when SNP chip genotypes are used instead of sequence data, which have very many low MAF SNPs, and when the GRM is based on Vanraden's method 1 instead of 2, since method 2 gives more weight to the low MAF SNPs.

Under inbreeding and random mating and random selection, the Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies are expected to be redistributed towards , , and . This allows for the estimation of inbreeding from the (loss of) heterozygosity, which is reduced by a factor . Assuming the current allele frequency is , and drift is , the Hardy-Weinberg expected genotype frequency of the 'AA' genotype in generation t is:where  is the variance of the allele frequency changes and since  in the absence of selection. Equating  to its expected redistributed frequency: , yields an inbreeding estimate based on the drift-variance: . However, if SNP alleles and/or genotype frequencies are affected by either genomic selection or genomic inbreeding management, this affects the redistribution of the Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies, and the above heterozygosity and drift-based estimates of inbreeding are no longer valid. However, under SNP based selection, A and Gla relationships are still expected to be unbiased, since calculation of A does not involve SNPs and SNPs are only used to infer paternal/maternal inheritances in Gla, i.e. actual frequencies are not used. Selection for SNP-alleles does not bias their paternal/maternal inheritances, and Gla based relationship management is neutral with respect to allele frequency changes. To avoid selection biases, it also seems beneficial that FGla does not use IBS information of SNP genotypes of animals separated by several ungenotyped generations to estimate paternal/maternal inheritance probabilities, which information would be used in more comprehensive linkage analyses.
Conclusions

FGla is an approximate computationally efficient algorithm for linkage analysis based relationship and inbreeding coefficients estimation, which brings together established phasing and linkage analysis methods in a novel combination, enabling the analysis of large, practical data sets. It requires > 3 generations of genotyped individuals, and approaches an accuracy of 0.998 as the number of genotyped generations increases. The Gla relationship matrix is particularly suited for optimal contribution selection as: (1) Gla is (semi-)positive definite; (ii) Gla based inbreeding management is neutral with respect to allele frequency changes; (iii) Gla has a well-defined base population, namely the founder animals of the pedigree (same as A); (iv) Gla yields a consistent relationship matrix across genotyped and non-genotyped animals, i.e. it allows for non-genotyped selection candidates; and (v) Gla relationships are unbiased estimates of true relationships in the BLUP sense, i.e. if Gla predicts an increase in relationships then on average an identical increase in true IBD relationships will occur.
